summary: Definitive and progressive sanctification; the Spirit’s work; the believer’s responsibility; growth in holiness
readingInstruction: Read Romans 6:1-14, 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8, and Philippians 2:12-13. Today is a doctrinal pause on sanctification: how God makes believers holy. Notice who acts and what the believer is told to do.
settingTheScene: After chapters on justification and a chapter on the war within, Romans moves toward the Spirit’s work in chapter 8. Today we pause to ask: if we are justified by faith alone, how does a Christian grow? The New Testament uses the word sanctification to describe the process of being made holy, set apart for God and conformed to the image of Christ. Paul wrote to the Thessalonians, a young church in a pagan city, to urge them to live in holiness. And to the Philippians he gave the famous pairing of God’s work and ours.
observation: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions” (Romans 6:12).
“But present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life” (Romans 6:13).
“For sin will have no dominion over you, since you are not under law but under grace” (Romans 6:14).
“That, as you received from us how you ought to walk and to please God, just as you are doing, you do so more and more” (1 Thessalonians 4:1).
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3).
“For God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness” (1 Thessalonians 4:7).
“Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12).
“For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).
doctrinalFocus:
Sanctification is the work of God by which he makes believers holy. The Bible speaks of it in three ways. First, definitive sanctification: at conversion, every believer is set apart for God. Paul calls the Corinthians “sanctified in Christ Jesus” even while he rebukes them (1 Corinthians 1:2). Second, progressive sanctification: throughout life, the Spirit conforms us to Christ, so that we put to death the old ways and grow in love, joy, peace, patience, and the rest of the fruit of the Spirit. Third, final sanctification: when Christ returns, we will be made perfectly like him (1 John 3:2).

The key to Philippians 2:12-13 is that both are true at once. “Work out your own salvation” does not mean earn it; it means carry it into every area of life. And the reason is: “for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work.” God’s work does not replace ours; it empowers it. We are active, but we are not alone. This is why Christians pray, read, fight sin, and serve, and then give God the credit.

Sanctification differs from justification. Justification is a legal declaration, once for all and complete, while sanctification is a lifelong process that is never completed in this life. Justification is wholly God’s act, while in sanctification we cooperate by the Spirit’s power. But they cannot be separated. Everyone whom God justifies, he sanctifies. Holiness is not a condition for being accepted; it is the fruit of being accepted.

The ordinary means of sanctification are the word of God, prayer, the fellowship of the church, the Lord’s Supper, and suffering. Christians differ about whether believers can reach a state of entire sanctification or sinless perfection in this life. Wesleyans hold that perfect love is possible; Reformed Christians hold that sin remains until death while the Spirit’s work grows. All agree that the call to holiness is real and urgent, and that no one can see the Lord without it (Hebrews 12:14).
interpretation:
In Romans 6:12-14, Paul uses commands that rest on the facts of union with Christ. Do not let sin reign. Do not offer your members to sin. Offer yourselves to God. The ground of obedience is grace: “You are not under law but under grace.” The law could command but not empower. Grace both forgives and strengthens. This is why the New Testament never treats holiness as a condition of salvation but always as its result.

In 1 Thessalonians 4, Paul writes to young believers who have turned from idols. “This is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God.” Sanctification is concrete. It touches our bodies, our habits, our relationships. And Paul adds that “God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness. Therefore whoever disregards this, disregards not man but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.” The Spirit is the Holy Spirit, and he is the one who makes us holy. Notice that Paul urges them to do this “more and more.” Growth is expected.

The pairing in Philippians 2 is the most balanced summary. “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” The phrase conveys reverence, not terror. And then the encouragement: God is the one at work in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. Even the desire to obey is his gift. This should keep us from pride when we obey and from despair when we fail.

So what do you do? Fight sin by the Spirit, using the means of grace. Remember who you are in Christ. Confess when you fall, and get up. And trust the one who began a good work in you to bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).
connection: 1 Corinthians 1:2 and 6:11 speak of being sanctified. John 17:17 is Jesus’ prayer, “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.” Romans 8:13 says by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body. Galatians 5:16-25 describes walking by the Spirit. 2 Corinthians 3:18 says we are being transformed into the same image. Hebrews 12:1-14 speaks of strife toward holiness. 1 Peter 1:13-16 calls us to be holy as he is holy. 1 John 3:2-3 gives the final hope. Ezekiel 36:27 promises the Spirit to cause us to walk in his statutes.
application:
Choose one specific area of obedience to work on this week. Ask the Spirit for help, and tell someone who will ask you about it.

When you obey, thank God. When you fail, confess and move on. Neither pride nor despair.

Read Philippians 1:6 as an encouragement that God will finish what he began.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for setting you apart in Christ.
Ask him to work in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure.
Tell him where you want to grow.
